## Network-Based Scholarly Discovery and Knowledge Mapping

This community studies large information networks—especially citation, coauthorship, patent, university, and multilingual Wikipedia graphs—to measure influence, reveal communities, and improve discovery. A dominant theme is ranking: PageRank, CheiRank, weighted variants, reduced Google matrices, and interactive author–paper models are used to distinguish prestige from popularity, assess universities and researchers, trace geopolitical and cultural relationships, and identify emerging technologies. Citation-network studies also address credit for datasets, first-author bias, patent-cluster growth, and the evolution of scientific communities.

Typical methods combine graph theory and scientometrics with centrality analysis, community detection, stochastic block models, network flows, spectral/eigenvalue analysis, and statistical comparisons. Temporal datasets and longitudinal snapshots support studies of career development, collaboration, citation dynamics, and Wikipedia’s multilingual structure. Information-retrieval work adds discipline-specific query expansion, knowledge maps, metadata linking, user-behavior signals, and integrated digital libraries. Data quality is treated through author disambiguation and inter-assessor reliability analysis.

Recent trends emphasize massive, heterogeneous, and multilingual networks; reduced-matrix and visualization techniques for interpreting indirect interactions; prediction of future community or technology growth using LSTM models; graphon-based modeling of large networks; and broader recognition of datasets and linked research artifacts as first-class scholarly contributions.

## Community Detection Across Complex, Dynamic Networks

This community focuses on defining, detecting, evaluating, and exploiting community structure in complex networks. Major themes include the ambiguity of what constitutes a “good” community; comparisons using multiple criteria, Pareto optimality, modularity variants, conductance, and quality metrics for fuzzy or overlapping groups; and taxonomies for selecting algorithms according to network properties.

Methods span stochastic block and geometric block models, spectral and local spectral clustering, modularity and multislice modularity optimization, density-based clustering with manifold learning, label propagation, clique percolation, motif counting, cores and k-trusses, and personalized PageRank diffusions. Theoretical work examines detectability thresholds, metastable dynamics, localization, neighborhood communities, bridges, and the role of degree heterogeneity.

Increasing attention is given to richer data: weighted, attributed, signed, two-mode, multiplex, multilayer, and public-private graphs. These settings motivate probabilistic models, variational inference, multilayer clique methods, and joint treatment of shared and layer-specific communities. Dynamic-network research addresses evolving layouts, temporal importance, and bibliometric change.

Recent directions emphasize scalable local methods for very large graphs, inclusive assignment of low-degree nodes, automated algorithm selection, active learning, privacy-preserving community deception, and applications to peer influence, churn, adoption, Web services, and information extraction.

### Collaborative Web Knowledge and Semantic Search

This community studies how user-generated content—especially Wikipedia, Wiktionary, folksonomies, social bookmarks, and professional networks—can support knowledge organization, search, recommendation, and expertise discovery. Major themes include extracting structured data from collaborative resources; transforming Wiktionary into machine-readable dictionaries; analyzing Wikipedia categories, links, authors, and multilingual entity annotations; and representing folksonomies through thesauri, ontologies, SKOS, and “folksodriven” networks.

Typical methods combine large-scale corpus and clickstream analysis with graph mining, clustering, centrality and ranking algorithms, co-occurrence statistics, power-law and growth modeling, NLP, ontology matching, entity linking, and learning-to-rank. Systems use Wikipedia’s link and category structure for semantic navigation, synonym expansion, entity ranking, and news discovery. Collaborative behavior is analyzed through tagging distributions, vocabulary growth, group-search properties, collective attention, and social influence.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes scalable, multilingual and language-agnostic processing, including densely annotated Wikipedia and high-throughput entity disambiguation. Search is becoming more personalized and socially informed through collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, inferred intent, homophily, and ideal-candidate search. Evaluation and deployment concerns also grow: unbiased click-based preference collection and recognition of societal and data-induced bias in recommender systems are prominent newer directions.

### Explainable Predictive Coding and Data-Driven Forensics

This community centers on machine-learning methods for large-scale document analysis, especially legal document review. Its primary themes are predictive coding for identifying relevant or privileged electronically stored information, reducing review costs, and improving attorneys’ trust in automated classification through explainability.

Typical methods include supervised text classification using Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, Convolutional Neural Networks, and other deep-learning approaches. The studies emphasize empirical comparisons across algorithms, evaluation on multiple real-world legal reviews with varying document lengths, and investigation of how preprocessing parameters affect model effectiveness. Explainable classification and case-based demonstrations address the perception of predictive coding as a “black box.”

A related theme applies analytics to cybersecurity forensics: archived Google Analytics data—including visitor location, timestamps, webpages, and search keywords—is used to monitor web activity and understand potentially malicious cyber actors.

Recent trends include movement beyond static preprocessing and single-algorithm workflows, increased experimentation with deep learning and CNNs, testing on realistic document collections rather than only short texts, and stronger emphasis on interpretable outputs for professional decision-making.

## Data Management, Search, and Responsible Ranking

This community focuses on scalable data management and information access across relational, spatial, multimedia, graph, and web databases. Major themes include flexible querying over uncertain or incomplete data, including fuzzy summaries, fuzzy SQL, incomplete-data skylines, aggregate skylines, and experiential search. Search and recommendation research addresses ranking, re-ranking, tag and expert recommendation, and fairness for protected groups, with work on demographic-aware MMR, bias measurement, and antidote data to reduce polarization.

Typical methods combine specialized indexing and query algorithms—locality-sensitive hashing, spatial indexes, bitmap and Roaring indexes, set-intersection structures, skyline and pruning algorithms, and hidden-database crawling. Compression is a recurring systems concern, with SIMD-based integer coding, variable-byte encoding, difference-Huffman coding, and histogram-aware bitmap ordering. Systems increasingly exploit parallel hardware and distributed execution, including CPU/GPU spatial processing, GPU transaction engines, and Spark/Flink-based graph mining.

Recent directions emphasize socially responsible retrieval, explicit treatment of ambiguity and missing values, and practical acceleration for large-scale workloads. Graph and workflow search introduce structural models and efficient ranking, while learned query planning seeks to improve graph-database performance. Overall, the work bridges theoretical query processing with deployable, hardware-conscious systems.

### Collaborative Web Knowledge, Search, and Networked Information

This community studies how user-generated Web resources support information organization, retrieval, and discovery. Major themes include Wikipedia and Wiktionary as news, lexical, encyclopedic, and semantic resources; collaborative tagging and folksonomies; search and ranking for Web and library systems; and social or professional networks as sources of expertise, influence, and talent-flow evidence.

Typical methods combine large-scale corpus and clickstream analysis, power-law and growth modeling, graph centrality and clustering, co-occurrence-based semantic similarity, HITS/PageRank-style ranking, query expansion, learning-to-rank, and meta-evaluation of search metrics. Structured knowledge extraction is prominent: Wiktionary entries are transformed into relational schemas, Wikipedia categories and links support entity ranking and semantic navigation, and annotated multilingual text enables entity linking. Ontology matching, SKOS encoding, and SPARQL access connect these resources to the Semantic Web.

Recent work emphasizes scalable, multilingual, language-agnostic processing of user-generated data, including high-throughput entity disambiguation and linking. Search is becoming more user- and task-centered through collaborative search, ideal-candidate queries, expertise location, and improved library catalogs. Evaluation research seeks lower-cost test collections via intelligent topic selection, while network studies increasingly analyze influence, collective attention, and career mobility.

**Cognitive and Social Recommender Systems**

This community studies recommender systems that combine behavioral, cognitive, temporal, and social signals. A major theme is social tagging: researchers model human memory and activation processes to improve tag and hashtag reuse, recommendation, and user acceptance. Frequency, recency, semantic context, forgetting, and lexical–semantic representations are incorporated through ACT-R-inspired models such as BLL and its extensions. These methods are evaluated across folksonomies, Twitter, bookmarking, and annotation datasets, often against popularity-based, collaborative-filtering, and graph-ranking baselines.

A second theme is social recommendation for marketplaces, music, jobs, classifieds, and general resources. Work exploits friendships, trust, weak ties, location, transactions, ratings, and social-commerce interactions to address sparsity and cold start. Typical methods include user- and item-based collaborative filtering, social regularization, regular equivalence, hybrid models, pre-filtering, embeddings, deep learning, and scalable service architectures. Studies use offline metrics, semantic similarity, diversity and novelty measures, online click-through rates, and Mechanical Turk or field experiments.

Recent directions emphasize real-time deployment, neural/item embeddings, fairness in music recommendation, explainable cognitive dynamics, and combining multiple social and contextual data sources rather than optimizing accuracy alone.

**Geographical, Temporal, and Context-Aware Recommendation**

This community focuses primarily on personalized point-of-interest and venue recommendation in location-based social networks, with one broader contribution extending matrix factorization. Central themes include alleviating sparse check-in data and modeling users’ preferences through geographical proximity, mobility, temporal activity, venue popularity, contextual appropriateness, social signals, reviews, and categorical information.

Typical methods combine collaborative filtering or learning-to-rank with auxiliary context. Matrix-factorization approaches use Euclidean metric factorization, logistic objectives, and joint geographical–temporal modeling. Collaborative-ranking models incorporate multiple location-based similarities, geographical influence, and two-phase temporal regularization. Other work uses probabilistic mappings between user tags and location taste keywords, dimensionality reduction, and scoring functions based on venue content, reviews, user context, and social information.

Recent directions move beyond exact check-in matching and static distance assumptions. Models increasingly capture time-dependent geographical effects, local geographical structure, popularity and activity variation, and richer venue semantics. Neural representation learning is also emerging through POI embeddings that combine sequential behavior with categorical information, complementing established factorization and ranking techniques.

### Decentralized and Peer-to-Peer Social Networks

This community investigates decentralized online social networks (DOSNs) as alternatives to centralized platforms such as Facebook and Twitter. Its central themes are user privacy, data sovereignty, security, autonomy from service providers, resistance to censorship, scalability, and service availability. A recurring concern is how to preserve availability and usability when users retain control of their own data.

Typical methods include comprehensive surveys of P2P-based social networks; architectural design of distributed platforms; and explicit definition of system goals, threat models, and trust models. Proposed infrastructures include general peer-to-peer frameworks and super-peer architectures. The papers also examine mechanisms for establishing global policies across independently controlled networks and identify requirements for viable P2P social-network systems.

Recent work trends toward practical and resilient designs rather than solely motivating decentralization. In particular, researchers emphasize highly available services, resilient architectures, data-availability guarantees, and policy coordination in decentralized environments. Overall, the community moves from diagnosing the privacy and control limitations of centralized OSNs toward developing distributed frameworks capable of competing with established social-network applications.

### Semantic Discovery, Retrieval, and Scientific Novelty

This community focuses on computational methods for navigating rapidly expanding scholarly and patent literature, while studying how novelty shapes scientific impact. Major themes include content-based paper recommendation, interactive exploration, document similarity, astronomy knowledge discovery, and patent retrieval/prior-art search.

Typical methods apply machine learning, text-based similarity, embeddings, word-position information, and high-dimensional stochastic block models. Systems emphasize scalable, near-real-time retrieval and recommendation, with applications including PubVis, Science Concierge, Mr. DLib, and automated patent prior-art search. Evaluation uses large publication, patent, and grant datasets, citation dynamics, user clicks, and comparative baselines.

A parallel research thread examines novelty and surprise: machine learning quantifies grant novelty and relates it to later citations, while predictive models identify unexpected combinations of content and context associated with outsized impact. Recent trends therefore move beyond keyword search toward semantic, full-text, and interactive discovery; open-source and real-world evaluation; and large-scale predictive analysis of scientific trajectories. Patent retrieval remains a central information-retrieval task, increasingly automated to reduce the time and errors of manually constructed keyword queries.

## Scalable and Semantically Rich Data Management

This community studies how database systems can scale across multicore, distributed, cloud, and data-intensive scientific environments while preserving transactional guarantees. Major themes include high-contention OLTP, MVCC, snapshot isolation, distributed consistency, replication, and recovery. Proposed techniques include parallel and adaptive command logging, application-semantic recovery, conflict repair, decentralized timestamps, relaxed write rules, Paxos-based protocols, and formal consistency checking and testing.

A second theme is data-intensive scientific and spatial analytics. Relational backends, array extensions, metadata and provenance management, batch scheduling, multidimensional indexes, hierarchical triangular meshes, zones, and relational spatial algebra support astronomy, simulations, and large social-network datasets. Systems such as LifeRaft and LiveGraph improve locality and throughput for analytical workloads.

The community also explores alternative architectures: actor databases, predictable virtualized reactors, automatic application partitioning, NUMA-aware stream processing, flat combining, and log-structured storage. Energy-aware query and cluster optimization reflects operational concerns, while ChainifyDB and immutable-data indexes address blockchain-style integrity and versioning.

Recent trends emphasize exploiting hardware locality and application semantics, integrating transactional and analytical processing, reducing coordination and logging overhead, supporting exascale scientific data, and making database behavior observable through provenance, reenactment, and systematic consistency testing.

### Knowledge Compilation for Probabilistic Query Evaluation

This community studies exact inference for unions of conjunctive queries (UCQs) over tuple-independent probabilistic databases. A central theme is the relationship between **extensional** evaluation—exploiting query structure directly, often with inclusion–exclusion—and **intensional** evaluation, which compiles query lineages into tractable Boolean representations before computing probabilities.

Knowledge-compilation formalisms are examined through structural properties such as decomposability, determinism, and structuredness, alongside circuit width measures including treewidth and pathwidth. The papers develop systematic upper and lower bounds connecting bounded-width circuits to structured representations such as deterministic structured NNFs and OBDDs.

Typical methods include lineage construction, weighted model counting, Boolean circuit transformations, and decision-DNNF/FBDD comparisons. Lower-bound results clarify limitations of propositional approaches and the representation complexity of exact model counting, with direct implications for probabilistic databases.

Recent work trends toward unifying width parameters with compilation classes and constructing deterministic decomposable circuits in polynomial time for important classes of “safe” queries. Together, these results investigate when intensional compilation can match or complement extensional query evaluation and where fundamental representation barriers remain.

### XML Structure, Indexing, and Distributed Querying

This community focuses on efficient management and querying of large, heterogeneous XML collections. A central theme is **structural summarization**: DescribeX supports declarative, XPath-based descriptions of complex and heterogeneous document structures, while path-summary research develops practical construction and exploitation algorithms, particularly with path-partitioned storage, to optimize data access.

A second major theme is **distributed XML management in peer-to-peer networks**. ViP2P uses DHT overlays and distributed materialized XML views to share and query document corpora. LiquidXML extends this direction with adaptive redistribution of XML fragments, including overlapping or redundant placement, so storage and processing can respond to workload and network conditions.

The papers typically employ declarative XPath or XML query specifications, structural summaries, materialized views, path partitioning, DHT-based distribution, and adaptive data-placement strategies. Evaluation is grounded in query-processing performance, supported by algorithms and experiments.

Recent trends move from centralized indexing toward heterogeneous, distributed, and adaptive architectures. They also emphasize improving result quality: XML keyword-search research identifies the limitations of local LCA/SLCA/MLCA filtering and advocates globally examining structural consistency to eliminate spurious results more reliably.

### Diffusion, Influence, and Dynamics in Social Networks

This community studies how information, behaviors, products, and infections propagate through evolving social and interaction networks. Major themes include source and start-time identification from partial cascades; recovery of hidden network structure and edge-infection probabilities; cascade structure, popularity, attention, affect, and engagement; and the roles of external agents, mass media, absent nodes, and indirect co-location links.

A second strong focus is intervention: influence maximization, worker recruitment, viral marketing, network design, and activity shaping through incentives. Work addresses adaptive decisions under myopic feedback, competing products, threshold adoption, collective diffusion, and non-submodular cascades. Related studies examine community structure, group centrality, topic-based influence, and collective intelligence in changing networks.

Typical methods combine diffusion, epidemic, threshold, independent-cascade, Hawkes-process, and continuous-time models with optimization, approximation guarantees, mixed-integer programming, greedy or community-based heuristics, random walks, particle-swarm search, and provable recovery analyses. Large-scale empirical studies mine Twitter, YouTube, Yelp, scholarly graphs, and software repositories, using cascade traces, text, profiles, video memes, and engagement measures.

Recent directions emphasize adaptive rather than fixed interventions, richer temporal and heterogeneous networks, content-aware and semantic signals, aggregate or incomplete observations, and modeling exogenous forces alongside endogenous social spread.

### Privacy-Preserving Data Analysis and Sharing

This community centers on enabling useful analysis of sensitive relational, graph, mobility, and behavioral data while limiting disclosure. A dominant theme is differential privacy, spanning histograms, range and predicate queries, marginal statistics, frequent-itemset mining, clustering, decision trees, data exploration, data cleaning, recommendation, and hierarchical population estimates. A parallel theme examines weaknesses of anonymization, including re-identification, membership and attribute disclosure, background knowledge, algorithm-aware adversaries, and reconstruction attacks.

Typical methods include calibrated noise, hierarchical decompositions, wavelet transforms, adaptive data- and workload-aware partitioning, matrix mechanisms, strategy-query optimization, and local differential privacy. Other approaches include k-anonymity variants, slicing, randomization, synthetic data, surrogates for protected graphs, provenance views, and privacy-preserving federated or encrypted query processing using secure hardware.

The work increasingly prioritizes utility, scalability, and workload awareness rather than privacy alone: algorithms seek near-optimal error for high-dimensional or correlated queries, sparse data, and large-scale exploration. Applications broaden toward location recommendation, mobility release, fair decision-making, data cleaning, and federated medical analysis. At the same time, papers emphasize stronger threat models—including worst-case background knowledge—and practical systems that make privacy guarantees usable without requiring analysts to manage complex mechanisms themselves.

## Querying, Ranking, and Scalable Data Systems

This community spans advanced database querying, information retrieval, and data-intensive system optimization. A major theme is flexible search over complex or imperfect data: fuzzy databases and linguistic summaries support vague information; skyline, aggregate skyline, and incomplete-stream queries address multi-criteria decisions; and keyword search extends to relational object summaries, hidden web databases, workflows, and labeled graphs.

Ranking is increasingly treated as a user- and society-sensitive task. Work on query reranking, tag and expert recommendation, and third-party reranking services adapts results to user preferences. Fairness studies quantify demographic bias and introduce fair reranking, diversity-aware recommendation, image-based representations, and “antidote” data; related analysis examines representation and proxy bias in bios.

A second strong theme is scalable execution. Methods include SIMD and variable-byte compression, bitmap and Roaring indexes, set-intersection algorithms, histogram-guided sorting, learned graph query planning, and GPU/CPU-hybrid execution for transactions and spatial operations. Distributed in-memory dataflow supports frequent subgraph mining, while MapReduce enables large-scale wavelet histograms.

Recent directions emphasize practical acceleration on modern hardware, compact indexing, graph- and workflow-aware retrieval, learning-assisted optimization, and explicit fairness and polarization objectives in recommendation.

### Educational Data Mining for Student Success

This community focuses on applying educational data mining (EDM) and learning analytics to improve higher education, particularly in India. Central themes include predicting student performance, distinguishing high and low performers, identifying students at risk of dropout, and supporting institutional decision-making. Other applications include examining classroom teaching language and attendance, detecting abnormal examination or grade data, identifying unfair means in online examinations, and predicting course enrollment.

Typical methods involve extracting hidden knowledge from growing educational databases through supervised classification and predictive modeling. Bayes-based classification and decision-tree classifiers are specifically emphasized, alongside comparative studies and experimentally constructed datasets. These models generate actionable predictions for incoming or currently enrolled students and can guide interventions intended to improve performance and reduce attrition.

The papers also frame EDM as an emerging intersection of education, information and communication technology, and data mining. A survey of learning analytics highlights increasing interest in frameworks, integrated models, and data-mining techniques for understanding and improving learning outcomes. Overall, the recent trend is a shift from general advocacy for educational data use toward learning-analytics systems and targeted predictive applications for student support and institutional quality improvement.

## Topic Modeling and Social Media Intelligence

This community centers on extracting structured knowledge from large, dynamic, and multimodal social and textual data. Major themes include topic discovery and evolution, event detection and summarization, social-media recommendation and user-interest modeling, spatial-temporal analysis, and information extraction for domains such as public health, disasters, tourism, libraries, and online news.

Typical methods include probabilistic topic models (LDA, PLSA, hierarchical and dynamic Dirichlet processes), multi-grain modeling, topic-based graphs, and semantic networks. Researchers combine these with TF-IDF, keyword-volume analysis, clustering, neural networks and embeddings, ontology similarity, fuzzy logic, and machine learning. Event-oriented studies exploit temporal bursts, power-law and self-similarity properties, geo-tagged streams, and multimodal text-image evidence. Other work emphasizes scalable processing, summarization, visualization, ranking, and actionable knowledge.

Recent trends move toward real-time and continuous analysis of high-volume streams; dynamic models that capture topic birth, death, and popularity; distributed topic learning; character-based and neural representations for noisy multilingual tweets; and richer fusion of textual, visual, geographic, and temporal signals. Applications increasingly support operational decision-making, including crisis response, disease surveillance, misinformation analysis, environmental warnings, and social-action monitoring.

**Personalized Recommendation Under Sparse and Changing Feedback**

This community focuses on recommender systems for large-scale e-commerce and two-sided marketplaces, particularly travel and accommodation platforms. Core themes include preference-aware ranking, matching guests with suitable accommodations while serving provider goals, and the pervasive user- and item-cold-start problem.

Typical methods combine latent-factor recommendation models with content-based prediction. For new items, convolutional neural networks infer latent factors from item descriptions when interaction data are unavailable. Deep learning is also examined for candidate generation and as a broader framework for recommender-system design. The work emphasizes practical evaluation, including large-scale online experiments against production systems rather than relying solely on offline comparisons with random or popularity-based baselines.

A notable recent trend is moving beyond the conventional one-time cold-start setting. The “continuous cold start” perspective recognizes that even known users and items may have sparse, outdated, volatile, or persona-dependent histories. Consequently, recommendations increasingly seek to exploit broader interaction data and contextual or content signals when personal history is unreliable. Overall, the papers reflect a shift from static collaborative filtering toward robust, scalable ranking and matching systems capable of personalization with limited or changing feedback.

### Social Media as a Lens on Spatial and Social Behavior

This community studies how social-media and mobile data can reveal human behavior, places, and relationships. Major themes include geolocation inference; urban mobility, activity regions, boundaries, and visited-place semantics; spatially embedded social and contact networks; and location-based applications such as business-site selection, recommendations, advertising, and emotionally pleasant routing. Other work examines social influence, political prediction, event outcomes, group scheduling, food culture, sexual-violence reporting, and urban affect, sound, and smell.

Typical methods combine natural-language processing, sentiment and semantic analysis, supervised classification, convolutional and other deep-learning models, probabilistic and Gaussian-mixture approaches, low-rank approximation, density-based spatial clustering, graph representation and feature extraction, and network analysis. Researchers exploit tweets, check-ins, geotagged photographs, reviews, Facebook and Instagram activity, telecommunications records, and crowdsourced perception data. Large-scale mining is frequently paired with surveys, travel diaries, smellwalks, or independent datasets for validation.

Recent directions emphasize inference without explicit geotags, quantified uncertainty and standardized evaluation, scalable distributed trajectory analysis, multimodal and cross-platform data integration, correction of social-media sampling bias, and out-of-sample validation. The work also increasingly moves beyond prediction toward interpretable urban experiences—mood, beauty, quietness, soundscapes, smellscapes—and practical decision support for cities, businesses, and public-health applications.

## Social Networks, Opinion Dynamics, and Network Optimization

This community studies how network structure, interpersonal influence, and online information shape behavior. Major themes include opinion formation and polarization (DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, bounded-confidence, biased, multi-topic, and signed-network models), diffusion and influence maximization for products, ideas, and public information, and strategic network formation involving centrality, PageRank, communicability, and discoverability. Other work addresses link prediction, backbone discovery, temporal event mining, web crawling, and topic-specific social-media behavior.

Typical methods combine graph theory, Laplacian and spectral analysis, dynamical-systems stability and convergence proofs, game-theoretic equilibrium and complexity analysis, optimization, and probabilistic or mean-field models. Empirical studies mine voting records, Twitter and other interaction data, while scalable algorithms use spectral embeddings, network motifs, and efficient sampling.

Recent directions emphasize signed and antagonistic interactions, feedback between recommendation systems and evolving opinions, dynamic or interdependent networks, and explicit modeling of controversy, fragmentation, and echo chambers. Fairness is increasingly central: studies examine equitable influence maximization, algorithmic mitigation of homophily-driven fragmentation, and bias across network positions in cyberbullying detection. Overall, the work moves from static structural measures toward adaptive, data-informed, socially aware network control and inference.

## Schema.org Semantics, Validation, and Scalable Knowledge Graphs

This community primarily studies how Schema.org annotations can make web content machine-readable and actionable. Major themes include domain-specific semantic modeling, annotation quality, scalable publication of dynamic data, and the use of structured data in tourism. Several papers define tourism domains and build a Tyrolean tourism knowledge graph by mapping heterogeneous sources into Schema.org and exposing them through graph-based applications.

Typical methods include domain specifications that select appropriate Schema.org types and properties; formal customization using SHACL operators; verification against vocabulary and domain constraints; and validation against the underlying web-page content. Other work develops context-dependent publication heuristics to control performance, latency, capacity, and disclosure when publishing changing data. Platforms support annotation creation, publication, and distribution, while Schema.org action annotations enable automated Web API consumption and personal-assistant workflows.

The community’s broader systems perspective considers graph databases for sensor-surveillance data and compares NoSQL and NewSQL approaches for big-data management and scalable OLTP. Recent trends move beyond search-engine visibility toward machine-readable services, automated actions, formal quality assurance, domain-tailored schemas, and integrated ecosystems for producing and consuming structured knowledge.

## Scientometrics, Scholarly Visibility, and Research Evaluation

This community studies how scientific impact, visibility, use, and quality can be measured across publications, authors, venues, publishers, and institutions. Major themes include validating altmetrics against peer assessments and societal-interest tags; comparing Google Scholar, Web of Science, Scopus, and specialized databases; assessing books, monographs, publishers, and research units; and examining open access, preprints, downloads, readership, and social-media activity as complements to citations. Scholarly communication is also investigated through venue recommendation, academic profiles, web linking, editorial-board networks, and science-park interactions.

Typical methods combine large-scale bibliometric and webometric data with citation, download, loan, readership, tweet, review, and hyperlink analysis. Statistical correlation, regression, factor analysis, ranking, longitudinal comparison, and indicator benchmarking are common. Network analysis, visualization, text and review mining, information retrieval, machine learning, and integer programming support mapping, matching, recommendation, and bibliographic disambiguation.

Recent work emphasizes heterogeneous and potentially dependent altmetric data, the early prediction of citation impact from usage, the effects of open access and arXiv dissemination, and systematic cross-database comparisons. It also advances automated conference classification and reviewer assignment, richer book and publisher indicators, and user-centered measures such as co-readership and online engagement.

## Network Diffusion, Influence, and Epidemic Control

This community studies how information, influence, disease, and failures propagate through social, technological, biological, and cyber-physical networks. A major theme is **diffusion inference**: locating one or multiple sources from partial cascades, recovering hidden network structures, estimating edge-infection probabilities, and learning contagion dynamics from aggregate observations. Related work develops diffusion and superposition distances, cascade models, and contrastive learning over directed spanning trees.

A second theme is **influence maximization and intervention**. Papers select seeds, marketing strategies, workers, or containment resources to maximize spread, adoption, revenue, or coverage. Methods include adaptive and myopic greedy policies, submodularity and adaptivity-gap analysis, community-based heuristics, random walks, continuous-time Markov chains, mixed-integer programming, and particle-swarm optimization. Several studies distinguish influence from actual adoption and incorporate incentives, online activities, or resource constraints.

The community also analyzes **epidemic cost, stability, and resilience**, using random-matrix theory, message passing, stochastic spreading models, and optimization for temporal, adaptive, and interdependent networks.

Recent directions emphasize partial and aggregate observations, time-varying or continuous-time diffusion, complex contagion, mobile or external spreaders, self-healing infrastructure, and learning-based cascade modeling, alongside scalable sampling and query methods for large evolving network data.

## Software, Data, and Reproducible Scholarly Communication

This community examines how research software and data can become visible, citable, reusable, and credit-bearing components of scholarly communication. Major themes include extending citation graphs to software and dependencies, developing reliable software and data citation practices, measuring software impact, and addressing the reproducibility of computational research. The papers also highlight sociotechnical barriers: inconsistent terminology, incomplete citation standards, and academic incentive systems that undervalue software and data contributions.

Typical methods combine conceptual and infrastructure design with empirical analysis. Researchers propose graph models incorporating software and transitive credit, survey academic researchers about data-sharing practices, analyze thousands of Zenodo DOI citations, and investigate citation-based impact measurement through the `lme4` R package. Other work reviews reproducible-publishing infrastructures and describes publication initiatives such as JOSS and ReScience.

Recent trends point toward open-science requirements from funders, journals, and reviewers; formal DOIs for software versions and concepts; dedicated journals and repositories; and stronger expectations that code, data, and execution environments accompany computational results. Overall, the community is moving from advocacy for reproducibility toward institutionalized infrastructures and measurable recognition for research artifacts.

## Scientometrics, Citation Networks, and Research Evaluation

This community focuses on measuring, mapping, and evaluating scientific activity through bibliometric data. Major themes include field and technology delineation; institutional, national, journal, and author performance; citation impact and academic reputation; research-front evolution; and the social and policy consequences of assessment systems.

Typical methods combine citation, co-citation, bibliographic-coupling, author–paper, and journal–journal networks with clustering, centrality measures (including PageRank and the K-index), overlay maps, and similarity or cognitive-distance measures. Researchers develop and compare field- and time-normalized indicators, especially percentiles, percentile classes, I3, SNIP, h-index variants, fractional counting, and contribution-sensitive measures. RPYS and related visualization tools reconstruct intellectual histories and research fronts, while MeSH and publication data support alternative knowledge representations.

Recent work emphasizes validation, fairness, and comparability: testing the universality and statistical interpretation of indicators, quantifying uncertainty in institutional comparisons, correcting normalization and database-linkage problems, and accounting for large collaborations. Studies also examine how digital dissemination weakens the journal impact factor’s relation to article citations, compare Dimensions with Scopus and Web of Science, and investigate diversity, national assessment policies, conference publishing, and emerging interdisciplinary fields.

## Social Media Networks, Polarization, and Information Integrity

This community centers on computational analysis of online social platforms, especially Twitter, to study political behavior, polarization, misinformation, extremism, and platform security. Key themes include community and belief-structure discovery, voter and demographic preference inference, echo chambers, propaganda, rumor and fake-news diffusion, and the behavior of fringe communities such as Gab. Other work addresses spam, autogenerated content, malicious nodes, Sybil attacks, privacy, and crowdsourced-system vulnerabilities, alongside applications in public health, disasters, and hydroinformatics.

Typical methods combine network analysis of retweets, follows, mentions, and interaction patterns with machine learning and statistical modeling. Nonnegative and structured matrix factorization, PCA, LDA, sparse learning, regression, embedding-based user modeling, semi-supervised detection, and deep neural networks are used for clustering, stance and rumor detection, preference inference, and user classification. Several studies model propagation, segregation, conflict, credibility, and intervention dynamics, while others develop real-time systems, sampling strategies, and browser or bot-based tools.

Recent trends emphasize early and message-level misinformation detection, propagation-aware and multimodal signals, quantitative separation of data and ranking bias, overlapping rather than strictly divided beliefs, cross-platform political campaigns, and targeted interventions against harmful content or behaviors.

## Data-Driven Personalization in Online Fashion

This community focuses on improving online fashion discovery, assortment planning, and purchase confidence through personalized, data-driven systems. Key themes include complementary-item recommendation, customer and product style modeling, demand-aware merchandising, dynamic preferences, and footwear fit for users without purchase history.

Typical methods combine behavioral, sales, and product-content signals. ZSF-c develops a personalized, session-based complementary recommender with a training-sample strategy designed for noisy interaction data. Fashion DNA uses deep neural networks over article tags and images, trained to predict sales, producing product and customer-style vector spaces for purchase-likelihood estimation and article mapping. An LSTM-based dynamic customer model addresses changing inventories, trends, and customer preferences using large-scale sales backtesting. Other work derives a style quotient that separates stylistic demand from commercial effects to support assortment breadth and depth, with backtested demand and prediction errors. A production-oriented footwear system targets online fit guidance, including customers with no prior purchases.

Recent trends emphasize neural and representation-learning approaches, integration of content with sales data, temporal adaptation, practical handling of sparse or noisy behavior, and broader personalization beyond ranking—extending to merchandising decisions and product attributes such as size.

## Data Management for Uncertain, Causal, and Inconsistent Information

This community studies database systems that move beyond deterministic, perfectly consistent data. A major theme is probabilistic and uncertain databases: query answering, aggregates, joins, top-*k* ranking, similarity search, and scalable processing under tuple independence, correlations, continuous distributions, and Markov views. Typical methods include relational encodings (U-relations), structural decompositions, knowledge compilation, lifted inference, probabilistic pruning, and approximate query plans with provable bounds.

A second theme is explanation and causality. Provenance, lineage, data differencing, Shapley values, actual causation, responsibility, and causal effect quantify why answers—or non-answers—occur and support debugging, auditing, reproducibility, and fairness analysis. Answer-set programs and abductive diagnosis connect causality with repairs and view updates.

The community also addresses inconsistency and incomplete information through repairs, active integrity constraints, belief annotations, conceptual dependencies, certain answers, and semantic query optimization. Work on XML policy repair, peer-to-peer exchange, schema mappings, and ontological data quality extends these concerns across heterogeneous systems.

Recent directions emphasize practical scalability and user interaction: massive probabilistic databases, database-native approximate inference, interactive relational browsing, performance explanation for MapReduce, and context-dependent quality assessment. Foundational results continue to map tractability and undecidability frontiers for query answering, determinacy, boundedness, and probabilistic computation.

### Recommender Systems: From Collaborative Filtering to Adaptive, Responsible Ranking

This community centers on predicting user preferences and sequential behavior across products, media, news, travel, and education. Foundational approaches include matrix factorization, slope-one predictors, neighborhood methods, Markov chains, content similarity, ontologies, and social or trust-based graphs. Hybrid models combine long-term preferences with short-term transitions, metadata, temporal signals, and multimodal content.

A major theme is sequential and session-based recommendation, including latent-state models, recurrent networks, context trees, playlist continuation, inter-session modeling, and graph neural networks such as SR-GNN. Neural methods increasingly learn nonlinear user–item interactions through variational autoencoders, neural collaborative filtering, factorization machines, DeepFM, metric learning, and mixture-of-tastes representations. Recent work also addresses missing modalities, cold start, shared accounts, cross-domain behavior, and complex user interests.

The community emphasizes recommendation quality beyond accuracy: popularity and long-tail exposure, diversification with personalized reranking or determinantal point processes, and the effects of social influence. Robustness and trust appear in studies of shilling attacks, rating reliability, reputation, and offline-evaluation bias. Emerging operational goals include online experimentation, revenue-aware ranking, and reinforcement learning for advertising while preserving user experience.

## Scholarly Information Retrieval, Networks, and Research Infrastructures

This community studies how scholarly information is organized, discovered, evaluated, and credited. Major themes include bibliometric and citation analysis; coauthorship and collaboration networks; author-name disambiguation and metadata record linkage; and interactive retrieval tailored to task, topic, and discipline. Other work addresses knowledge maps, Semantic Web knowledge-organization systems, linked-data enrichment, and integrated digital libraries for research data.

Typical methods combine graph analysis and network science—PageRank and weighted variants, centrality, modularity-based community detection, network flow, brokerage/closure models, and bipartite author–paper representations—with information-retrieval evaluation, query expansion, and user-behavior signals such as search sessions and mouse fixations. Studies also use labeled datasets, simulation, triangulated evaluation, statistical agreement measures, PCA, interviews, ethnography, and visual scientometric mapping.

Recent directions emphasize more reliable and reproducible scholarly data: validating disambiguation methods, cleaning noisy PDF metadata, assigning credit to datasets, and using notebooks and linked data. Research increasingly treats infrastructures and governance as socio-technical concerns, including open and grey data, privacy, preservation, and long-term maintenance. Emerging user-facing work explores visual and collaborative digital libraries, publication recommendation from citation behavior, and neural title simplification to improve scientific visibility.

## Semantic and Linked Digital Mathematics Knowledge

This community focuses on making mathematical knowledge machine-readable, interconnected, and interactively usable. Major themes include Mathematical Knowledge Management (MKM), semantic authoring and formalization, collaborative repositories, and digital mathematics libraries. Projects such as SWiM and the OpenMath wiki support community editing of OMDoc-based content dictionaries, while Math-Net.Ru and proposed reference DML architectures address large-scale archival access.

Typical methods combine domain ontologies, semantic markup, and Linked Data. LaTeX and lecture notes are enriched with Semantic LaTeX, RDFa, XHTML, and MathML, enabling metadata-rich browsing, querying, and links to external resources. Ontology-driven platforms such as OntoMath integrate document-structure and mathematical-knowledge models with text analysis and recommender tools. Flexible vocabulary-based relationships also support multidimensional classification in software-engineering documents.

A prominent trend is moving beyond static digitization toward active knowledge ecosystems: distributed repositories, interoperable OpenMath content dictionaries, and semantic annotations exposed as Linked Data. Interactive interfaces help learners and researchers explore corpora, while the Planetary system extends this vision to executable papers whose results can be checked, manipulated, and explored. Overall, the work emphasizes scalable formalization, community participation, semantic interoperability, and richer computational access to mathematical literature.

## Social Networks, Trust, and Commerce

This community examines how social relationships shape online marketplaces, recommendations, and consumer behavior. A central theme is integrating marketplace activity with social-network and location-based data to recommend products, categories, and items, while addressing sparsity and cold-start problems. Trust is treated as both explicit ratings and implicit social connections; regular equivalence and weak ties are used to extend collaborative filtering beyond directly similar users.

Several studies empirically analyze social commerce, including information exchange and transaction behavior on Taobao and the transformation of friends and family into sellers on Beidian. Other work measures social influence, comparing friend recommendations with aggregate ratings and finding asymmetric effects of negative and positive opinions. Complementary research models rumor dissemination through desires, trust networks, social homogeneity, and convergence.

Typical methods include graph and triadic analysis, collaborative filtering, social-feature integration, user studies, computational modeling with convergence results, and deployed systems. Recent trends emphasize combining heterogeneous data sources, exploiting weak ties and trust, building scalable service-oriented recommendation engines, and designing usable, private social-commerce platforms such as Serefind.

## Community Detection in Complex and Evolving Networks

This community centers on defining, detecting, and evaluating mesoscopic structure in complex networks. Major themes include the ambiguity of “good” communities; comparison of partitions using multi-criteria, Pareto-optimal, modularity-based, and overlapping quality measures; and classification or selection of algorithms according to network properties. Core–periphery organization, polarization in signed graphs, low-degree-node inclusion, and stability of centrality are recurring structural concerns.

Typical methods range from label propagation, modularity optimization, density-based clustering, manifold learning, clique percolation, local spectral expansion, and core decomposition to stochastic block models, geometric block models, random-matrix analysis, and variational Bayesian inference. Several studies develop scalable or distributed approaches, including stabilized propagation and local algorithms for very large graphs.

A strong trend is modeling richer network structure: multiplex and heterogeneous layers, weighted and attributed nodes and edges, signed interactions, temporal evolution, and continuous-time tie dynamics. Dynamic visualization and evolving PageRank address changing networks, while adaptive edge weighting tackles modularity’s resolution limit. Applications span social influence, churn, smartphone adoption, online dating, recommendations, bibliometrics, Web services, and image segmentation. Increasing attention is also given to sampling bias, algorithm reliability, interpretability, and unbiased assignment of peripheral nodes.

## Durable, Contextualized Web and Scientific Archives

This community studies how to preserve, represent, search, and reuse evolving digital knowledge. Major themes include digital-object repositories and life-cycle modeling; long-term preservation of heterogeneous, distributed, and compressed artifacts; and provenance, versioning, annotation, and formal representation of scientific claims. A strong focus is web archiving: estimating resource age, acquiring and parsing mementos, measuring link and content loss, understanding archive use, and supporting temporal search over large collections. Linked Open Data preservation and schema reconciliation extend these concerns to evolving datasets and scientific entities.

Typical methods combine standards-based architectures and ontologies (Fedora, aDORe, OAIS, SharedCanvas, Open Annotation, PAV, nanopublications) with repository implementations, APIs, query languages, and SPARQL services. Empirical studies use access logs, longitudinal web-archive samples, social bookmarks, tweets, and Wikipedia edits. Retrieval and collection systems employ focused crawling, caching, federated search, machine learning, ranking, and graph analysis.

Recent work emphasizes fresh event-oriented collections integrating social media, scalable temporal web-graph access, improved archive-service performance, and richer contextual metadata. It also highlights emerging risks: orphaned scholarly web objects, disappearing annotations and linked resources, evolving datasets, and the difficulty of producing trusted, repeatable timestamps for archived pages.

**Persistent and Heterogeneous Memory for Resilient Databases**

This community investigates how persistent and non-volatile memory (PM/NVM), alongside DRAM, SSDs, and other diverse devices, is reshaping database architecture. Core themes include persistent data structures, buffer management, I/O, storage placement, hashing, logging, recovery, and rapid restoration.

Typical methods combine performance evaluation on technologies such as Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory with new algorithms and system prototypes. Studies decompose data structures into reusable design primitives, characterize PM bandwidth and latency, and derive optimized primitives for log writing and block flushing. Other work develops multi-tier buffer managers, persistent buffer pools with optimistic consistency, and heterogeneity-aware storage management using semantic information rather than workload monitoring alone. Persistent hash tables target scalability, high load factors, and instant recovery.

Reliability is addressed through new failure models and recovery mechanisms: single-page failures motivate transactional page-recovery indexes, while redo-only recovery, fine-grained locking, and partial rollbacks support concurrent operation. Instant restore enables reads and writes during media repair by restoring requested segments on demand.

Recent trends move from isolated structures and emulated hardware toward holistic, real-device designs that exploit memory–storage duality, workload-aware hierarchies, instant recovery, and continuously available databases.

### Schemas, Validation, and Structured Data

This community studies how to describe, infer, validate, and efficiently query structured data across XML, RDF, web annotations, graphs, and tables.

A major theme is XML schema inference. Work learns deterministic, single-occurrence, unordered, and interleaving regular expressions from positive and negative examples, while characterizing learnability, minimality, and computational complexity. Related studies propose practical unordered-XML formalisms such as multiplicity schemas and analyze satisfiability, membership, containment, and query implication.

Another theme is schema-aware processing. Techniques use DTDs and types to schedule streaming event processors, minimize buffers, project irrelevant XML subtrees, rewrite XPath queries using views, and study containment and pattern-query complexity. Graph query research extends tree patterns with logical operators and develops labeling and decomposition methods for provenance and regular path queries, while also correcting assumptions in DAG pattern algorithms.

A substantial cluster focuses on Schema.org and RDF. It develops Shape Expressions, SHACL-based domain specifications, semantic verification and validation, ontology/content consistency checks, action annotations, and tools for publishing and consuming machine-readable web data. Tourism provides recurring deployment cases, including regional knowledge graphs and annotation ecosystems.

Recent work emphasizes domain-specific customization, automated validation, scalable publication of dynamic data, and practical knowledge-graph applications, alongside schema languages for tabular web data and broader graph/big-data management.

## Network Analysis of Fictional Narratives

This community studies fictional worlds through **character interaction networks**, representing characters as nodes and relationships—conversation, co-occurrence, friendship, or violence—as edges. Main goals include narrative summarization, subplot and role detection, classification, recommendation, and understanding social dynamics in novels, films, and television series.

Typical methods combine **manual annotation**, automated co-occurrence extraction, and machine-learning-based network construction. Researchers apply static and temporal social-network analysis to examine prominence, community structure, causality, changing roles, friendship patterns, and evolving subplots. Network properties are also used predictively, including models for forecasting killer–victim pairs in *Game of Thrones*. Comparative work evaluates how extraction choices affect network measurements and downstream interpretation.

Recent trends emphasize the **dynamic and longitudinal nature of serial narratives**, supporting summaries across seasons and analyses of changing character relationships. Several studies use prominent television series—including *Friends*, *Game of Thrones*, and other serial dramas—as case studies. The field is also expanding its empirical infrastructure through the *Serial Speakers* annotated multimedia dataset. Beyond relational structure, ecological diversity and Shannon-entropy measures are proposed to estimate effective cast size, classify films, and compare character composition across movies.

## Mining Topics, Events, and Knowledge in Dynamic Web Data

This community focuses on extracting structure and actionable insight from large, heterogeneous information sources. Major themes include latent topic discovery and evolution in document streams, hypertext, scientific literature, and online reviews; social-media analytics for event detection, summarization, sentiment, misinformation, and popularity; and recommendation of songs, microblogs, videos, and research papers. Scholarly applications address semantic publishing, author-contribution extraction, citation-sentence reuse, hypothesis generation, and scientific-article bundling.

Typical methods combine probabilistic topic models (LDA, PLSA, hierarchical and dynamic Dirichlet processes), clustering, TF-IDF and content similarity, graph and knowledge-base representations, ontology similarity with fuzzy logic, and information-extraction pipelines. Event systems use temporal and geospatial signals, sub-event detection, representative-tweet selection, power-law analysis, and text–image fusion. Neural networks, including CNNs and character-based embeddings, support recommendation and multilingual tweet clustering. Evaluation commonly relies on ranking experiments, comparisons with reference summaries, large-scale datasets, and expert or candidate-based validation.

Recent work trends toward real-time and scalable processing of streams, dynamic topic evolution, multimodal and geotemporal analysis, explainable recommendation, semantic linked data, and systems that support decision-making or creative discovery.

## Data Mining from Applications to Structured Data Exploration

This community surveys and develops data-mining methods for decision support across diverse domains. Applied studies address breast-cancer diagnosis and prognosis—distinguishing benign from malignant cases and predicting recurrence—and workforce demand forecasting in the Orissa Panchayat Raj Department. Broader survey work emphasizes data warehouses, large organizational datasets, managerial decision-making, and the expanding scope of data-mining techniques.

A recurring methodological theme is handling structured and relational data. Multi-relational data mining (MRDM) extracts patterns directly from multiple database tables, contrasting with propositionalisation into a single table. Complementary graph-based work uses Gaifman graphs to represent relationships in first-order or multirelational data. Modular decompositions, generalized quantitative Gaifman graphs, and 2-structure-based methods support exploratory analysis of relational patterns.

Recent work increasingly focuses on interpretable structural discovery and visualization. Clan decompositions provide hierarchical views of co-occurrence patterns; newly defined clan implications connect these decompositions to closure spaces and implication analysis. Algorithmic considerations and exploratory software implementation aim to make these methods practical. Overall, the community trends from conventional application-oriented prediction toward scalable, relational, graph-based, and visually interpretable data analysis.

## Network Diffusion, Influence, and Epidemic Control

This community studies how information, influence, disease, and failures propagate through social, technological, ecological, and cyber-physical networks. Major themes include influence maximization and marketing, epidemic modeling and containment, diffusion-source localization, hidden-network and parameter recovery, and diffusion over temporal, adaptive, or partially observed networks.

Typical methods combine probabilistic cascade models—independent cascade, linear threshold, SIS/SI, continuous-time Markov chains, and complex contagion—with graph algorithms and optimization. Researchers develop greedy, adaptive, and online policies; submodularity and adaptivity-gap analyses provide approximation guarantees. Other approaches include Jordan-center and covering methods for source detection, soft-thresholding and optimization for network inference, particle-swarm heuristics for estimating infection probabilities, message passing for interdependent systems, random-matrix analysis of epidemic costs, and mixed-integer programming for network design. Simulations on synthetic and real-world networks are common.

Recent directions emphasize adaptive decision-making with myopic or full feedback, dynamic and temporal network structure, collective or aggregate observations, fairness and profit-aware influence objectives, resource-constrained data collection, and explicit modeling of adoption, incentives, online activities, and socially salient groups. Applications increasingly extend beyond marketing to worker recruitment, conservation, public health, misinformation, and resilient infrastructure.

### Provenance and Scalable Interactive Analytics

This community studies how to make data analysis and visualization interactive despite expensive computation, large datasets, and complex workflows. A central theme is **provenance and lineage**: provenance can express visualization interactions and support extensible interaction systems, while fine-grained lineage captures relationships between individual workflow inputs and outputs for debugging, auditing, explanations, cleaning, and interactive analytics.

A second theme is **avoiding repeated work**. Compact provisioning constructs a polynomial-size sketch for answering queries across exponentially many hypothetical scenarios. Complementary work on transparent scaling seeks to let developers write visualizations naturally while automatically shifting computation to back-end services when browser resources are insufficient.

The papers use theoretical and systems-oriented methods: complexity and sketching arguments for provisioning; provenance-based formulations of visualization operations; workflow lineage capture and query support; and database execution-engine prototypes. Afterburner demonstrates in-browser analytics through compiled query plans, typed arrays, and asm.js, achieving performance comparable to native MonetDB on selected queries.

Overall, the research trends toward integrating database capabilities directly into interactive environments: provenance-aware visualizations, fine-grained lineage at interactive speed, transparent browser/back-end scaling, and increasingly capable browser-native analytical execution.

## Collaborative Web Knowledge and Semantic Networks

This community studies how user-generated content, links, tags, categories, and professional profiles can be transformed into searchable, structured knowledge. Major themes include Wikipedia and Wiktionary mining; folksonomy and collaborative-tagging behavior; Semantic Web interoperability and ontology matching; entity linking and disambiguation; collaborative and personalized information seeking; and analysis of social, attention, influence, and talent-flow networks.

Typical methods combine large-scale data extraction and parsing with graph-based analysis. Papers use co-occurrence statistics, power-law and allometric-growth models, clustering, centrality and HITS-like algorithms, matrix factorization, collaborative filtering, and learning-to-rank. Other recurring techniques include NLP-based relation extraction, multilingual translation resources, SKOS and relational schemas, category-based ranking, clickstream analysis, and visualization of semantic structures.

Recent work emphasizes scalable, multilingual, and production-oriented systems: densely annotated Wikipedia datasets, high-throughput language-agnostic entity linking, personalized expertise and talent search, and learning-to-rank for professional networks. Applications increasingly move beyond document retrieval toward forecasting locations, tracking job and talent flows, identifying influential users, and supporting product or candidate discovery. Overall, the research trends from describing emergent social metadata toward integrating heterogeneous user-generated signals into adaptive search, recommendation, and knowledge-representation systems.

## Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search and Graph-Based Retrieval

This community focuses on efficient similarity search and retrieval over large, high-dimensional or otherwise challenging datasets. Major themes include approximate \(k\)-nearest-neighbor (ANN) graph construction and merging, graph-based search for non-metric and asymmetric distances, and specialized indexing for binary codes and cosine similarity.

Typical methods include neighborhood-graph indexes, graph-search algorithms, locality-sensitive hashing (LSH), and angular multi-index hashing. Hybrid LSH methods target radius-neighbor reporting while reducing sensitivity to data- and query-dependent parameters, particularly under heterogeneous local densities. For binary vectors, angular multi-index hashing searches nearby hash buckets rather than scanning the full dataset. Graph methods can operate directly on non-metric or non-symmetric distances, while modified index-specific distances may improve performance.

The papers also address practical systems and evaluation. IDEL integrates neural entity linking into the MonetDB relational database through Python user-defined functions and machine-learning libraries. ANN-Benchmarks provides standardized interfaces, datasets, parameter testing, quality measures, and visualization for comparing in-memory ANN algorithms.

Recent trends emphasize combining complementary indexing strategies, supporting complex distance functions without costly transformations, integrating neural retrieval capabilities into databases, and improving reproducible, systematic benchmarking.

## Network Intelligence: Structure, Dynamics, and Trust

This community studies methods for understanding, predicting, and generating complex, social, temporal, and knowledge networks. Major themes include link prediction (including weighted, heterogeneous, continuous-time, and hidden criminal-network links), community detection and clustering, graph similarity, anomaly and fraud detection, and relationship profiling. Network representation learning is central, with surveys, evaluation benchmarks, and applications to urban dynamics, team composition, and financial risk.

Typical methods combine local structural signals—common neighbors, triangles, clustering coefficients, reliable routes, and connectivity—with probabilistic models, random walks, absorbing Markov chains, maximum likelihood, and scalable systems such as MapReduce. Machine learning approaches include random forests, neural and deep embeddings, metapath-guided cross-modal models, ensemble scoring, discriminative predicate paths, and approximate inference. Graph grammars and latent-space generative models support graph synthesis and dynamic-network modeling.

Recent directions emphasize temporal awareness: lossless temporal event representations, continuous-time relationship prediction, dynamic embeddings, offset reconstruction, and evolving community models. Other emerging concerns are robustness and trust, including privacy-preserving community deception, covert-network concealment, fraud de-anonymization, insider-trading detection, and privacy prediction. Work also increasingly integrates text and knowledge bases for entity normalization and fact checking, while pursuing principled sampling, uncertainty handling, probabilistic search, and domain-general evaluation.

again|f82f48cc682d84921557a8f301f39163af.text:
## Recommendation, Bias, and Dynamic Network Intelligence

This community centers on recommender systems and network-based information discovery, with particular attention to the social consequences of ranking. Major themes include popularity bias and long-tail exposure, fairness across demographic groups, recommendation diversity, and the trade-off between relevance, user utility, and business revenue. Researchers also study temporal effects, including item aging, recent behavior, forgetting, evolving popularity, and time-aware evaluation.

Typical methods include post-processing and personalized re-ranking, fairness-constrained ranking, diversity-weighted greedy optimization, temporal compensation, and antidote-data interventions. Network approaches model users and items as bipartite or signed graphs and apply random walks, diffusion, neighborhood similarity, and collaborative ranking. Bayesian Poisson factorization addresses sparse implicit feedback, while iterative reputation algorithms handle noisy ratings and spamming. Cognitive models such as ACT-R inform tag recommendation and reuse.

The community also develops supporting infrastructure and theory: offline-evaluation error analysis, reproducible recommender-system toolkits, hidden-database crawling, third-party query re-ranking, and streaming similarity joins. Applications span music, marketplaces, social tagging, search, crowdfunding, and push services. Recent work increasingly emphasizes fairness, demographic representation, polarization, long-tail coverage, and temporal dynamics, alongside scalable algorithms and realistic evaluation.

again|d7f63e3af79276d8da2b6893fd04112ff9.text:
## Graph-Based and Semantic Keyphrase Extraction

This community focuses on automatic keyword and keyphrase extraction, often to improve document discovery and relevance ranking in news aggregation and scientific text analysis. A related classification task assigns news articles to 12 categories, using more than 500,000 articles to support category-aware phrase extraction.

Graph representations are the dominant methodology. Text is modeled as complex networks, semantic-connectivity graphs, multipartite graphs linking candidate phrases and topics, or PageRank structures. These models rank candidate terms using node properties, contextual connections, mutually reinforcing topic relations, sentence position, and semantic roles. Both supervised and unsupervised approaches are represented: supervised systems learn keyword/non-keyword labels from graph-derived features, while unsupervised methods rely on graph scoring and ranking.

The community’s recent direction is toward richer linguistic and structural signals beyond word frequency or local co-occurrence. Proposed advances include parameterless graph construction, concept-level connectivity, explicit topical information, semantic-role knowledge, and mechanisms reflecting keyphrase selection preferences. Across the reported datasets and applications, these enhancements generally outperform established graph-based or state-of-the-art baselines.

again|4cb5b4d7397dab1ff30d054c371d6dabf9.text:
## Uncertainty, Privacy, and Explainable Graph Analytics

This community centers on reasoning over uncertain and evolving graph data. A major theme is **network reliability**: estimating s–t reachability, maximizing reliability under an edge-addition budget, and extending models to multiple terminals or condition-dependent edge probabilities. Related work addresses **node classification** and **similarity search** when links or sensor observations are unreliable.

A second theme is **privacy-preserving social graphs**. Papers use uncertainty semantics, probabilistic adjacency matrices, and noisy link exchange to obfuscate identities and relationships while preserving useful structural properties such as expected node degrees and local graph information.

The community also studies **interpretable graph and knowledge applications**. These include explaining relationships between entity pairs, contextualizing knowledge-graph facts with weak supervision, explaining how user actions relate to social feeds, tracing evolving news stories beyond simple similarity, and relaxing relationship queries when exact semantic associations fail.

Typical methods combine complexity and approximation analysis, sampling and indexing for #P-hard reliability estimation, probabilistic modeling, scalable graph search, anonymization schemes, and weakly supervised ranking or contextualization. Recent trends emphasize conditional uncertainty, scalable reliability optimization, uncertainty-aware learning, explainability, and privacy mechanisms that retain analytical utility.

again|c99e759e8a99a1ae3c9b5727cdd48ef867.text:
### Keyphrase-Centered Document Understanding and Summarization

This community focuses primarily on extracting, ranking, and generating keyphrases, keywords, and concepts for scientific, medical, news, broadcast, and social-media text. Applications include indexing, retrieval, categorization, tagging, title construction, summarization, news aggregation, and popularity prediction.

Typical methods combine lexical and statistical features—term frequency, inverse document frequency, position, readability, and stylometry—with supervised machine learning and neural networks. Graph-based approaches are especially prominent: PageRank, complex networks, multipartite graphs, dependency trees, semantic connectivity, semantic roles, and folksonomy graphs support candidate ranking, title compression, and tag recommendation. Hybrid systems combine statistical, graphical, and numerical signals, often using domain or category information.

Summarization research covers extractive single- and multi-document methods, hierarchical combinations of document summaries, keyword- and topic-based sentence selection, and privacy-preserving retrieval using Secure Binary Embeddings. Disaster hashtag identification and conceptual news representation extend extraction to social and multimedia monitoring.

Recent directions emphasize neural keyphrase generation, exemplified by the editor-curated KPTimes news dataset, alongside broader benchmarking that exposes weaknesses of complex models against simple baselines. Other trends include semantic and contextual enhancement of existing extractors, real-time processing, richer graph representations, and privacy-aware analysis of documents.
