## Recommendation Beyond Matrix Factorization

This community studies personalized recommender systems, with a strong emphasis on point-of-interest (POI) and venue suggestion in location-based social networks. Core themes include addressing sparsity, improving top-*N* ranking quality, and incorporating geographical, temporal, contextual, categorical, social, and content information.

Typical methods include collaborative filtering, matrix and logistic matrix factorization, metric factorization using Euclidean distance, and collaborative ranking. Researchers augment these models with location-based similarities, mobility patterns, popularity and activity variation over time, user context, venue reviews, tags, and categories. Probabilistic models, scoring functions, embeddings, and neural pre-training are also used for user and POI representation. Evaluation increasingly targets ranked recommendations and graded relevance rather than rating prediction alone.

Systems-oriented work examines parallel and distributed collaborative filtering, GPU-based *k*-nearest-neighbor search, and recommendation subgraphs for web navigation. Privacy is another concern, motivating selective preference-sharing frameworks for collaborative filtering.

Recent trends move from generic factorization toward context-sensitive and socially informed POI models, joint geographical-temporal modeling, category-aware neural embeddings, and direct optimization of ranked lists. Survey work highlights scalability, accuracy, sparsity, and privacy as continuing challenges.

again|b76856d281a04f846603f2ed93c06fee97.text:
**Principles and Systems for Scalable Data Management**

This community explores principled, high-performance data management across relational, graph, streaming, and machine-learning workloads. Core themes include query optimization and evaluation: MILP-based join ordering, worst-case-optimal and projected joins, inequalities, XQuery complexity, metaquerying, and dynamic or distributed conjunctive queries. Parallelism is studied through communication complexity, single-round correctness, coordination-free computation, MapReduce optimization, and hybrid relational execution engines.

A second theme is extending databases beyond traditional analytics. Relational systems support graph pattern matching and vertex-centric analytics, while specialized engines address visual content, time-series compression, approximate query processing, sampling, and fast-stream attention prioritization. Data quality, dataset versioning, metadata linkage, replication consistency, and divergent index tuning address practical lifecycle and governance concerns.

Typical methods combine formal complexity and correctness analyses with algebraic query transformations, worst-case bounds, sketches and sampling, probabilistic modeling, sparse tensors, matrix multiplication, and adaptive compression. Systems contributions emphasize declarative languages, high-level compilation, column stores, specialized hardware, and workload-aware optimization.

Recent directions increasingly integrate machine learning into database systems: end-to-end declarative ML, in-database inference and training, multi-tenant resource allocation, revenue-aware recommendation, and automated model calibration. Overall, the work seeks abstraction without performance loss while unifying data engineering, analytics, and learning.

### Scalable Text, Mathematical Retrieval, and Data Analytics

This community combines intelligent document analysis with high-performance data management. Research on text mining addresses probabilistic and hierarchical topic models, unsupervised and user-directed clustering, automated categorization, authorship classification, association-rule features, and quality-aware subject indexing. Typical methods include multinomial mixtures, k-nearest-neighbor and k-medoids classifiers, dependency-based pruning, hyperonymization, genetic feature selection, regression, and relevance feedback or continuous active learning.

A substantial theme is mathematical information retrieval. Systems combine textual and formula queries, compare presentation- and content-based representations, and use formula preprocessing, notation analysis, and identifier-definition extraction. Digital repositories and mathematical libraries support the indexing and reuse of mathematical objects.

Another major focus is scalable data infrastructure. Associative arrays unify spreadsheet, database, matrix, and graph views, while D4M, Accumulo, Graphulo, and BigSparse support high-rate ingestion and graph analytics. Related work develops polystore architectures, provenance storage, and external-memory processing.

Database studies emphasize memory-aware join costing, predicate optimization, relational-lattice algebra, progressive evaluation over uncertain data, and cloud workload management. Recent directions favor learning-based and adaptive systems: autonomous review, sentence-level feedback, deep quality estimation, reinforcement- or feedback-controlled scaling, and learning-based workload advisors, alongside increasingly semantic and content-aware mathematical search.

### Privacy-Preserving Data Publishing and Analysis

This community centers on enabling useful data release and computation while protecting individuals, organizations, and relationships. Differential privacy is the dominant theme, applied to sparse data, histograms, range and predicate queries, marginals, hierarchical statistics, clustering, decision trees, frequent-itemset mining, search logs, and recommendation. A parallel thread studies anonymization through \(k\)-anonymity, slicing, generalization, set-valued data, transparent mechanisms, and adversarial background knowledge, often emphasizing reconstruction and disclosure risks.

Typical methods add calibrated noise, use wavelet or hierarchical decompositions, privately learn data-dependent partitions, and optimize query strategies through the matrix mechanism or adaptive workload selection. Other approaches include local differential privacy, randomized perturbation, provenance views, surrogate graph elements, secure multiparty computation, query binning, trusted hardware, and synthetic data generation.

Recent work increasingly prioritizes utility, scalability, and workload awareness rather than privacy alone. This includes near-optimal batch and high-dimensional query answering, accuracy-aware exploration interfaces, private data cleaning, and domain-specific systems for mobility, location recommendation, federated databases, and fair allocation. The papers also show a shift toward stronger threat models—including algorithm-aware adversaries, worst-case background knowledge, and inference attacks—and toward evaluating privacy–utility–fairness tradeoffs in practical decision-making.

### Network Diffusion, Influence, and Opinion Dynamics

This community studies how information, opinions, products, infections, and failures spread through social, biological, cyber-physical, and uncertain networks. Major themes include influence maximization and worker recruitment; epidemic modeling, containment, and economic cost; source localization and hidden-network recovery from partial cascades; opinion formation under biases, antagonism, multiple topics, and recommender feedback; and reliability, resilience, and cascading failures in interdependent systems.

Typical methods combine threshold, independent-cascade, SIS/SI, DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, and continuous-time Markov models with graph theory, random matrix theory, factor graphs, and stochastic optimization. Researchers develop greedy and adaptive-submodular policies, community-based heuristics, mixed-integer programming, message passing, particle-swarm optimization, Jordan-center/cover algorithms, soft-thresholding, and estimation from vector autoregressive processes. Results frequently include NP-hardness analyses, approximation guarantees, stability and convergence conditions, recovery sample complexity, and simulation on synthetic and real networks.

Recent directions emphasize dynamics beyond static graphs: temporal, adaptive, spatial, and randomly evolving networks; myopic or partial feedback; competing products and complex contagion; external spreading agents; continuous-time diffusion; and interventions that actively modify network structure. Robustness and societal impact are also expanding, including self-healing cyber-physical networks, epidemic costs, political affinity inference, and closed-loop recommendation–opinion systems.

### Scalable Data Management, Query Processing, and Analytics

This community centers on building scalable, efficient, and intelligent data systems. A major theme is relational query processing: join ordering via mixed-integer linear programming, memory-aware cost models, worst-case-optimal and parallel joins, query evaluation with inequalities or projections, and formal analyses of query complexity and correctness. Learned methods increasingly address cardinality estimation, query optimization, approximate aggregation, and probabilistic summaries.

Graph analytics is another strong focus. Papers translate graph algorithms into relational joins and SQL, develop high-level engines such as EmptyHeaded, and explore specialized hardware and column stores. Large-scale distributed systems emphasize streaming updates, shared-nothing OLTP, multicore recovery, replication consistency, and parallel communication costs. Blockchain work examines atomic cross-chain transactions, emulation, and design differences from distributed databases.

Typical methods include deep neural networks, generative models, sparse tensors, MILP solvers, sketches and sampling, model-based compression, declarative languages, matrix multiplication, and benchmark-driven systems evaluation. Recent trends favor learned and approximate data management, end-to-end declarative data-science platforms, collaborative dataset versioning, high-level languages without performance loss, and hardware- or representation-aware acceleration for relational, graph, and visual workloads.

## Bibliometric Evaluation and Academic Research Systems

This community studies scientific performance, collaboration, and knowledge flows, with a strong emphasis on the Italian university system and comparisons across fields, regions, institutions, ranks, genders, and countries. Major themes include gender differences and recruitment bias, academic nepotism, the North–South divide, career seniority and aging, persistence of top-scientist status, and the effects of international and interdisciplinary collaboration.

Typical methods are large-scale bibliometric analyses of Web of Science and Google Scholar data, using publication, citation, h-index, field-standardized impact, and fractional or author-order-based indicators. Researchers apply regression, quantile regression, Granger causality, stochastic models, gravity models, network analysis, clustering, and distributional techniques such as Gini coefficients, characteristic scores, and funnel plots. Several studies address name disambiguation, counting methods, uncertainty, and cross-field comparability.

A recurring concern is the validity and fairness of evaluation systems. The papers critique journal impact factor, national assessment procedures, product selection, and university rankings, while proposing efficiency- and impact-oriented alternatives. Recent directions emphasize uncertainty-aware assessment, gender-adjusted rankings, editorial-board and co-authorship networks, geographic knowledge diffusion, interdisciplinary gains, and methods for overcoming incomplete data in publication recommendation and research measurement.

## Data Integration, Quality, and Crowdsourced Resolution

This community focuses on making heterogeneous, noisy data usable. Core themes include entity resolution and record linkage; data fusion and truth discovery across conflicting sources; entity consolidation into golden records; schema and structural understanding; integrity-constraint discovery; and data cleaning under uncertainty. Applications span Web and linked data, open-data platforms, social networks, government addresses, urban spatio-temporal data, and data exchange.

Typical methods combine blocking and similarity joins (locality-sensitive hashing, partitioning, string edit distance, and minimum-hash techniques) with probabilistic models, graph matching, collective message passing, and distributed representations such as DeepER and Column2Vec. Systems also emphasize scalable and progressive processing, parallelism, and adaptive scheduling. Constraint-based approaches discover or enforce functional, order, ontology, and denial constraints, while probabilistic repair supports exploratory analysis.

A strong theme is human involvement: crowd assessment, worker-error confidence intervals, low-latency labeling, route evaluation, and human–machine ER frameworks seek quality guarantees at controlled cost. Recent directions emphasize democratized and schema-agnostic ER, multiple-truth discovery, uncertainty and “unknown unknowns,” predictive spatial task assignment, on-demand cleaning, and platforms that incentivize data sharing and integration.

### Semi-Metric Networks and Adaptive Knowledge Systems

This community studies how non-metric, weighted, and proximity-based network structures can support information discovery and decision-making. A central theme is the relationship between fuzzy-graph transitive closures and distance-graph constructions, including alternative formulations of shortest paths beyond conventional metric closure and Dijkstra-based APSP.

Semi-metric behavior is exploited in recommender systems built from user–item co-occurrence and document networks, including the Web, digital libraries, and scientific databases. Experiments on MovieLens indicate that emphasizing highly semi-metric edges can improve recommendations over conventional item- and user-based methods.

Another theme is biologically inspired adaptation. Agent-based models of T-cell cross-regulation are applied to collective document classification, while distributed systems such as TalkMine and @ApWeb adapt keywords, resource structures, and communities through network-based learning.

Typical methods include weighted and fuzzy graph analysis, transitive closure, shortest-path computation, lightweight linear text models, word-proximity networks, uncertainty-based integration, agent-based simulation, and large-scale observational analysis of electronic health records. Applications increasingly connect abstract network theory with practical recommendation, biomedical text mining, distributed knowledge management, and population health, including the detection of demographic biases in drug-interaction administration.

## From Digital Objects to Linked Cultural Heritage Data

This community examines how libraries, archives, and museums define, preserve, model, and connect digital information. A central theme is the identity of information objects under changing carriers, migrations, and encodings. Ontological work seeks carrier-independent criteria for identifying objects, while a literature review surveys competing views on whether “significant properties” can—or should—be formally specified for preservation.

Several papers address the transition from traditional cataloging to the Semantic Web. They question the suitability of entity–relationship models for bibliographic data and explore RDF as a more flexible framework, while retaining the semantics of FRBR, FRAD, and related standards. One implementation proposal models theses and dissertations as autonomous metadata-based data, rather than merely descriptions attached to resources.

Typical methods are conceptual and ontological analysis, literature review, comparison of modeling frameworks, and prototype or implementation proposals. The pragmatic Linked Data discussion also highlights the practical and philosophical difficulties of applying Web principles in cultural heritage institutions.

Recent trends emphasize machine-processable metadata, RDF-based representations, linked data publication, and redesigned catalog structures, alongside continuing unresolved questions about object identity, preservation scope, and the formalization of meaningful properties.

**Efficient, Flexible, and Responsible Data Search**

This community advances database search, retrieval, and recommendation across heterogeneous, large-scale data. A major theme is flexible querying: fuzzy relational models, linguistic summaries, experiential search, incomplete-data skylines, aggregate skyline joins, and concise relational object summaries support imprecise information and multifaceted preferences. Search personalization is addressed through query/result reranking services, tag consistency, expert discovery, and workflow- and web-database search.

Efficiency is a persistent focus. Work develops bitmap and set-intersection structures, Roaring and threshold indexes, compact integer and multidimensional compression, SIMD optimization, hashing, locality-sensitive hashing, and learned graph query planning. Systems research exploits GPUs, multicore CPUs, distributed in-memory dataflow, and specialized in-memory indexing for OLTP, image comparison, and frequent subgraph mining.

A growing theme is socially aware retrieval and recommendation. Studies measure and mitigate demographic bias through fair reranking, diversity-oriented MMR, representation analysis, and “antidote” data, including high-stakes biography classification.

Typical methods combine formal query models and algorithmic complexity analysis with heuristic pruning, factorization and embeddings, tensor decomposition, association rules, re-ranking, and empirical system evaluation. Recent trends emphasize scalable hardware-conscious implementations, approximate high-dimensional search, learned optimization, fairness-aware ranking, and practical services that retrofit richer ranking preferences onto existing databases.
